name: Pyrenean ibex
intro: Zib! The Pyrenees mountains, 1910. Glorp's ears are popping! Up on these cliffs lives a wild goat with huge curved horns: the bucardo.
description: The Pyrenean ibex, or bucardo, was a wild mountain goat from the Pyrenees, the mountains between Spain and France. Males had thick horns that curved back in a wide sweep. It climbed steep, rocky slopes and grazed alpine meadows, moving lower in winter. Hunters prized its horns as trophies, and by the early 1900s only a small group was left. The very last one, a female named Celia, died in 2000 when a tree fell on her. Scientists had saved some of her cells, and in 2003 they cloned her: the baby was born alive but lived only a few minutes. It was the first time an extinct animal had ever been brought back, even briefly.

facts.diet: Grasses, herbs and shrubs; lichens in winter
facts.cause: Hunting (its horns were trophies) and competition with farm animals for grazing

habitat.biome: Rocky mountain slopes, cliffs and alpine meadows
habitat.climate: Cold winters with deep snow, mild summers

terrain.value: Steep rocky slopes with alpine meadows
terrain.why: It grazed high meadows and escaped predators by climbing cliffs.

temperature.why: Mountain winters are freezing and snowy, and even summer stays mild up high.

humidity.why: Mountain air changes from dry sunny days to cloud and snow.

oxygen.why: The air up here has the same mix of gases, just thinner.

pressure.why: It lived 1,000–2,800 m up, where the air pressure is much lower than at sea level.

hotspots.label: Rocky cliff
hotspots.fact: Bucardos climbed cliffs like this to escape wolves, and grazed the meadows below.

hotspots.label: Snow patch
hotspots.fact: Snow lingers up here into summer. Winters are freezing, so the ibex moved lower down the mountain.

hotspots.label: Passing cloud
hotspots.fact: One minute it's sunny and dry, the next a cloud rolls over the ridge and everything is damp.

hotspots.label: High peak
hotspots.fact: Glorp's ears popped on the way up: the air pressure up here is much lower than at sea level.

hotspots.label: Curved horns
hotspots.fact: A male's horns curved back in a wide sweep. Hunters wanted them as trophies, which is why so few bucardos were left.

hotspots.label: Young ibex
hotspots.fact: A kid, just a few months old, already climbing. Females usually had one kid each spring.

hotspots.label: Glorp's future note
hotspots.fact: The last bucardo, Celia, died in 2000. Scientists cloned her in 2003: the first extinct animal ever brought back, though the baby lived only minutes.
